blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — aseptic central-venous-catheter dressing change, skin antisepsis, glove selection, and sterile dressing
stem: A nurse is changing the transparent dressing on a stable central venous catheter in an adult client. Which technique best reflects current CDC catheter-site care guidance?

options.A: Use aseptic technique and >0.5% chlorhexidine in alcohol unless contraindicated; after hand hygiene, use clean or sterile gloves and apply a sterile dressing.
options.B: Use hand hygiene and sterile gloves, but omit skin antisepsis when the existing transparent dressing is intact and the insertion site has no redness or drainage.
options.C: Use maximal sterile barriers with cap, mask, sterile gown, sterile gloves, and a full-body drape for each routine dressing change, as for central-line insertion.
options.D: Use clean gloves and aseptic technique, cleanse the site with normal saline, and apply a clean nonsterile transparent dressing when no infection is visible.

rationale: A is correct. Current CDC intravascular-catheter guidance requires hand hygiene before and after dressing an intravascular catheter and maintenance of aseptic technique during catheter care. For dressing changes, either clean or sterile gloves may be worn. For central venous catheter dressing changes, clean skin should be prepared with a greater-than-0.5% chlorhexidine preparation with alcohol unless chlorhexidine is contraindicated, in which case CDC lists alternative antiseptics. The catheter site should be covered with sterile gauze or a sterile transparent semipermeable dressing. B is incorrect because an intact prior dressing and absence of local inflammation do not eliminate the recommended skin antisepsis during a dressing change. C is incorrect because maximal sterile barrier precautions are specified for CVC/PICC insertion or guidewire exchange, not every routine dressing change. D is incorrect because normal saline alone is not the recommended skin antiseptic for a routine CVC dressing change and the replacement dressing should be sterile.
educational_objective: Perform central-line dressing changes with hand hygiene and aseptic technique, appropriate chlorhexidine-alcohol skin antisepsis unless contraindicated, clean or sterile gloves, and a sterile dressing while distinguishing maintenance from insertion-level maximal sterile barriers.

correction_summary: Original Q0262 had a 234-character correct answer versus much shorter distractors. The item was rebuilt with four realistic dressing-change techniques. The key retains the exact CDC maintenance requirements while avoiding an unsupported claim that routine dressing changes require insertion-level maximal sterile barriers or that sterile gloves are mandatory when CDC permits clean or sterile gloves. Post-fetch refinement reduced the key from 174 to 158 characters to remove the remaining length cue. option_audit.A: Correct; matches CDC hand hygiene/aseptic technique, >0.5% chlorhexidine-in-alcohol antisepsis unless contraindicated, clean-or-sterile glove choice, and sterile dressing.
option_audit.B: Plausible near-correct sterile-glove approach; incorrect because skin antisepsis remains part of the dressing-change procedure.
option_audit.C: Plausible over-sterilization approach; incorrect because maximal sterile barriers are specified for insertion/guidewire exchange rather than every routine dressing change.
option_audit.D: Plausible low-risk maintenance approach; incorrect because saline alone is not the recommended skin antiseptic and the replacement dressing should be sterile.
